desc: Nature Medicine, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04768-x Several deaths during trials of experimental cell and gene therapies in China appear to reveal gaps in governance and oversight. title: Evaluation of a Rapid and Practical Deep Learning Framework for T1-weighted MRI-based Brain Age Estimation.
desc: [Radiology. Artificial intelligence] Purpose To develop and evaluate a rapid brain-age estimation framework using freely available Python tools and assess the clinical relevance of brain-age gap (BAG). Materials and Methods In this retrospective study conducted from March 2025 to August 2026, T1-weighted MR images from cohorts of cognitively normal adults (n = 4,346) were divided into training, validation, and internal test sets; two cohorts (n = 315 and 209) served as external test sets. Clinical evaluation used the BICWALZS cohort (n = 954; cognitively normal and various dementias). Preprocessing used freely available Python tools only. The model was trained to predict chronological age as the reference standard. Associations of the residualized BAG with diagnosis, amyloid PET positivity, white matter hyperintensity (WMH) severity, stroke history, and longitudinal clinical worsening were evaluated using ANCOVA, logistic regression, and Cox models. Results The development cohort included 4,346 cognitively normal adults (mean age, 47.0 ± 21.2 years; 2,414 women). Chronological age prediction yielded R2 = 0.95 and MAE, 3.76 years in the internal test set and R2 = 0.69-0.90 and MAE, 4.82-5.15 years in external test sets. The residualized BAG increased across diagnostic groups (P < .001) and was associated with WMH severity (odds ratio [OR], 1.64; P < .001) and stroke history (OR, 1.46; P < .001), but not with amyloid positivity after full adjustment (P = .17), and predicted longitudinal clinical worsening (HR, 1.92). Conclusion The framework accurately predicted age, while residualized BAG was associated with diagnosis, cerebrovascular burden, and longitudinal clinical worsening. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Cardiovascular Medicine: Advancing Diagnosis, Risk Stratification, and Therapeutic Decision-making.
source: PubMed · Cardiovascular & hematological disorders drug targets
desc: [Cardiovascular & hematological disorders drug targets] One of the main causes of death in the world is Cardiovascular Diseases (CVDs). The number of acute myocardial infarctions and fatalities may be considerably decreased by early detection of Cardiovascular (CV) events. However, the efficacy of conventional data analysis for diagnosis and treatment is hampered by the complexity of the disease and the wide range of affecting factors. Large, multidimensional medical datasets can be processed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) owing to its sophisticated computational capabilities. This narrative review was conducted through a structured search of PubMed/ MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar to identify peer-reviewed literature on artificial intelligence in cardiovascular medicine. Relevant studies addressing diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostic prediction, cardiovascular imaging, and clinical implementation were critically evaluated with emphasis on methodological quality, external validation, clinical applicability, and implementation challenges. AI-based systems have been shown to be more effective at classifying risk, predicting outcomes, and spotting illness trends. Early diagnosis and more customized treatment plans are made possible by these algorithms' ability to examine intricate relationships in large healthcare datasets. Clinical applications have improved auxiliary diagnostic instruments and increased patient care effectiveness. AI offers more accuracy and flexibility than traditional approaches when handling high-dimensional CVD data. It may reduce the burden of disease and promote tailored treatment regimens. However, data quality, standardization, and ethical concerns for broad use remain issues. The detection and treatment of CVDs are being revolutionized by AI-powered technology. Their use in clinical settings may improve cardiovascular care and lower the number of heart disease-related deaths worldwide.

title: AI-Based Digital Pathology Model for Predicting Treatment Response and Prognosis in mHSPC
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Xiangya Hospital of Central South University; conditions: Prostate Cancer, mCRPC (Metastatic Castration-resistant Prostate Cancer); type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 1115; status: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] The goal of this multicenter observational study is to develop and validate an artificial intelligence-based digital pathology model to predict treatment response and prognosis in adult men with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer treated with androgen deprivation therapy plus androgen receptor signaling inhibitors. The main questions it aims to answer are: Can digital pathology-based artificial intelligence predict deep prostate-specific antigen response, defined as prostate-specific antigen less than 0.2 ng/mL at 6 to 7 months after treatment? Can digital pathology-based artificial intelligence predict progression to metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and time to metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer? Researchers will compare artificial intelligence-defined low-risk and high-risk groups to evaluate whether the model can improve prediction of treatment response and prognosis beyond conventional clinicopathological risk stratification. Participants will not receive any additional intervention as part of this study. Researchers will retrospectively collect clinical characteristics, treatment records, prostate-specific antigen response data, follow-up outcomes, and archived prostate biopsy slides from participating centers. The biopsy slides will be scanned into whole-slide images and analyzed using artificial intelligence to develop and validate predictive models.

title: From Tool State to Scientific Action: Auditing Decision Provenance in Biomedical Research Agents
desc: A scientific agent can give the same verdict while reading and citing different evidence. BioAgent-DF tests this separation using paired reference and candidate values saved at the same scientific computation site. It restores or transplants those values at their original coordinates, then runs the agent on healthy hardware. Across eight SciFact batches, Qwen3.5-4B shows repeatable citation changes in three capture-claim combinations, and Gemma 3 4B IT shows repeatable read and citation changes in four. These seven combinations cover two claims. Full restoration recovers the reference evidence sets while verdicts remain unchanged. Verdict changes observed under the baseline prompt did not recur under the explicit-example prompt. Complementary tool and optimizer experiments distinguish recovery of numerical state, recovery of ranked lists, and restoration of an agent's visible history. These results show that an audit should track both the evidence an agent uses and its final answer. In hERG cardiac-safety assay allocation, silent numerical faults changed testing decisions while the fixed-budget shortlist kept the same number of compounds labeled as blockers. After the agent had used faulty values, restoring its earlier execution state and supplying certified scores recovered all 39 changed decisions, whereas replacing the prediction file recovered none; no incorrect action was committed. A streaming implementation of the arithmetic checks reduced the total time for forward execution and verification by 42.4% relative to the original FP64 implementation, with identical flags and recovery outputs.

title: EvoSurv: Evolution-Aware Multimodal Survival Modeling Reveals Complementary Prognostic Signals
desc: Accurate cancer survival prediction remains challenging due to tumor heterogeneity. Although multimodal survival models integrate clinical and molecular data, they often overlook evolutionary information encoded in genomic alterations. To address this gap, we developed eTime, a 38-dimensional evolutionary representation comprising eight feature groups that characterize clonal and subclonal mutation burden, mutational spectra, functional consequences, copy-number alterations, and anoikis-related genomic changes. We further developed EvoSurv, a multimodal survival framework integrating eTime with clinical variables and RNA expression. Across six TCGA cancer cohorts comprising 2,782 patients, EvoSurv achieved the highest mean concordance index (C-index) in all six cancers, averaging 0.663 and outperforming three state-of-the-art survival prediction methods. More importantly, we assessed whether evolutionary features provide additional prognostic information beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors. eTime remained significantly associated with survival in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) and liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) after adjustment for clinical variables and RNA-derived risk scores. Feature-group analyses further revealed cancer-specific prognostic patterns. In HNSC, T>G substitutions were associated with increased mortality risk after clinical and molecular adjustment, including in HPV-negative patients, with supporting evidence from an independent CPTAC-HNSCC cohort. Overall, these findings demonstrate that eTime captures survival-associated evolutionary information and highlight its potential to provide prognostic value beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors.

title: RawMod: Modification-Agnostic Detection of DNA Base Modifications from Nanopore Signal Pileups
desc: Summary: Identifying epigenetically modified bases (e.g., methylation) is crucial for many important applications such as discovering mechanisms of cancer development, cell differentiation, and bacterial defense. Nanopore sequencing generates electrical signals that can differentiate canonical bases from modified ones. To detect base modifications from signals, machine learning (ML) methods and statistical approaches are commonly used. These methods can either detect a specific modification type or require an additional unmodified copy of the same DNA as a control group. However, no released model detects modification types beyond those it was trained for, which makes it difficult to detect rare modification types without an unmodified control. Our goal is to accurately identify the presence of modified sites regardless of their modification type, which we define as modification-agnostic detection. To this end, we propose RawMod, a transformer-based modification-agnostic and control-free method for detecting epigenetically modified genomic positions. The key idea of RawMod is to compare the raw signals of many reads at each site with the unmodified reference sequence, using a small model that learns many modification types as a single modified class. Based on our extensive evaluations on the detection of various modification types (5mC, 5hmC, 4mC, 6mA, and 5hmU) using various genomes, RawMod achieves the highest mean AUROC across modifications compared to control-based methods and control-free modification models. A single RawMod model with 0.23M parameters detects five modification types with a mean AUROC of 0.964, against 0.799 for the best released model. When a modification type is withheld from training, RawMod still detects it (AUROC 0.91--0.98), provided another modification of the same base was seen in training. We use RawMod to map 5hmU without a control across a 7.7 Mb contig of the Amphidinium carterae genome, consistent with two published trends. Further, we show that the modification-aware embeddings from RawMod can be used to differentiate read origin (e.g., cell types, tumor/normal origin, and native/PCR-amplified DNA). We discuss how RawMod can enable further work on label-free classification of cell types using these modification-aware embeddings. title: Automated MRI-Based Segmentation of the Cranio-Cervical Venous System Using a Dedicated Deep Learning Pipeline
desc: PURPOSE To develop an automated magnetic resonance imaging based segmentation pipeline for the cranio-cervical venous system (CCVS), a complex anatomical network for which no dedicated segmentation tool is currently available. MATERIALS AND METHODS A retrospective single-center cohort of 194 contrast-enhanced cranio-cervical MRI examinations acquired between 2019 and 2024 was used. Manual reference segmentations were performed on 50 examinations using 3D Slicer. A nnU-Net v2-based segmentation model was trained through an iterative process combining automatic segmentation, manual correction, and retraining. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). The complete processing pipeline was integrated into an open-source software application, VenousNetworkAnalyzer (VNA). RESULTS The final model achieved a mean DSC of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.95) in five-fold cross-validation on 106 examinations with manual reference segmentations. Iterative optimization progressively reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours of fully manual segmentation to less than 10 minutes of manual correction per patient. Application of the final model to the entire cohort enabled the generation of patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions of the cranio-cervical venous system. The segmentation workflow was successfully integrated into the VNA software environment, allowing automated processing and visualization of MRI datasets. CONCLUSION This study demonstrates the feasibility of automated segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system from contrast-enhanced MRI using a dedicated deep-learning pipeline. The resulting reduction in processing time and integration into an open-source software platform provide a foundation for future large-scale anatomical studies of cranio-cervical venous draina
